title: Post-Quantum Commitments
statement_text: A post-quantum commitment scheme ⟨ C, R ⟩ is a classical interactive protocol between interactive PPT machines C and R . Let m ∈ {0,1} ^ ℓ (λ) (where ℓ ( · ) is some polynomial) is a message that C wants to commit to. The protocol consists of the following stages: Commit Stage: C(m) and R interact with each other to generate a transcript (which is also called a commitment) denoted by τ , C 's state ST _ C , and R 's output b_ com ∈ {bot ,top } indicating acceptance (i.e., b_ com =top ) or rejection (i.e., b_ com =bot ) . We denote this execution by (τ, ST _ C ,b_ com ) gets ⟨ C(m), R ⟩ (1^λ) . When C is honest, ST _C is classical, but when we consider a malicious quantum committer C^*(ρ) , we allow it to generate any quantum state ST _ C^* . Similarly, a malicious quantum receiver R^*(ρ) can output any quantum state, which we denote by OUT _ R^* instead of b_ com . Decommit Stage: C generates a decommitment decom from ST _C . We denote this procedure by decom gets C( ST _C) . Then it sends a message m and decommitment decom to R , and R outputs a bit b_ dec ∈ {bot , top } indicating acceptance (i.e., b_ dec =top ) or rejection (i.e., b_ dec =bot ) . We assume that R 's verification procedure is deterministic and denote it by Verify (τ,m, decom ) . Note that Verify is well-defined since our syntax does not allow R to keep a state from the commit stage. W.l.o.g., we assume that R always rejects (i.e., Verify (τ, · , · ) = bot ) whenever b_ com = bot . (Note that w.l.o.g., τ can include b_ com because we can always modify the protocol to ask R to send b_ com as the last round message.) The scheme satisfies the following requirements: (Completeness.) For any polynomial ℓ : N → N and any m ∈ {0,1} ^ ℓ (λ) , it holds that Pr [b_ com =b_ dec =top : l (τ, ST _ C , b_ com ) gets ⟨ C(m),R ⟩ (1^λ) decom gets C( ST _C) b_ dec gets Verify (τ,m, decom ) ] = 1. (Statistically binding.) For any unbounded-time committer C^* , the following holds: Pr [ l ∃ m_0,m_1, decom _0, decom _1, s.t. m_0 ≠ m_1 ∧ Verify (τ,m_0, decom _0)= Verify (τ,m_1, decom _1)=top :(τ, ST _ C^* ,b_ com ) gets ⟨ C^*, R ⟩ (1^λ)]= negl (λ). For any non-uniform QPT receiver R^* and any polynomial ℓ : N → N , the following holds: { OUT _ R^* ⟨ C(m_0),R^* ⟩ (1^λ) }_ λ ∈ N , m_0, m_1 ∈ {0,1} ^ ℓ (λ) stackrel c ≈ { OUT _ R^* ⟨ C(m_1),R^* ⟩ (1^λ) }_ λ ∈ N , m_0, m_1 ∈ {0,1} ^ ℓ (λ) , where OUT _ R^* ⟨ C(m_b),R^* ⟩ (1^λ) (b ∈ {0,1} ) denotes the output of R^* at the end of the commit stage.

label: def:VSS
title: Verifiable Secret Sharing
statement_text: An (n + 1, t) -perfectly secure VSS scheme Π _ VSS consists of a pair of protocols ( VSS _ Share , VSS _ Recon ) that implement respectively the sharing and reconstruction phases as follows. Sharing Phase VSS _ Share : Player P_ n+1 (referred to as dealer) runs on input a secret s and randomness r_ n+1 , while any other player P_i (i ∈ [n]) runs on input a randomness r_i . During this phase players can send (both private and broadcast) messages in multiple rounds. Reconstruction Phase VSS _ Recon : Each shareholder sends its view v_i (i ∈ [n]) of the Sharing Phase to each other player, and on input the views of all players (that can include bad or empty views) each player outputs a reconstruction of the secret s . All computations performed by honest players are efficient. The computationally unbounded adversary can corrupt up to t players that can deviate from the above procedures. The following security properties hold. if the dealer is dishonest, then one of the following two cases happen (i.e., with probability 1): During the Sharing Phase, honest players disqualify the dealer, therefore they output a special value bot and will refuse to play the reconstruction phase; During the Sharing Phase, honest players do not disqualify the dealer. Therefore such a phase determines a unique value s^* that belongs to the set of possible legal values that does not include bot , which will be reconstructed by the honest players during the reconstruction phase. Secrecy: if the dealer is honest, then the adversary obtains no information about the shared secret before running the protocol Recon . More accurately, there exists a PPT oracle machine S ^ ( · ) such that for any message m , and every (potentially inefficient) adversary A corrupting a set T of parties with |T| ≤ t during the Sharing Phase VSS _ Share (m) (denote A 's view in this execution as View _ A , T (1^λ, m) ), the following holds: { View _ A , T (1^λ, m)} stackrel i.d. =mathrel mkern -3mu = { S ^ A (1^λ, T)} . Correctness: if the dealer is honest throughout the protocols, then each honest player will output the shared secret s at the end of protocol Recon .

statement_text: A post-quantum batch commitment scheme ⟨ C, R ⟩ is a classical interactive protocol between interactive PPT machines C and R . Let vb m =(m_1,...,m_n) ∈ {0,1} ^ ℓ (λ) × n(λ) (where ℓ ( · ) and n(λ) are some polynomials) be a sequence of messages that C wants to commit to. The protocol consists of the following stages: Commit Stage: C(vb m ) and R interact with each other to generate a transcript (which is also called a commitment) denoted by τ , C 's state ST _ C , and R 's output b_ com ∈ {bot ,top } indicating acceptance (i.e., b_ com =top ) or rejection (i.e., b_ com =bot ) . We denote this execution by (τ, ST _ C ,b_ com ) gets ⟨ C(m), R ⟩ (1^λ) . When C is honest, ST _C is classical, but when we consider a malicious quantum committer C^*(ρ) , we allow it to generate any quantum state ST _ C^* . Similarly, a malicious quantum receiver R^*(ρ) can output any quantum state, which we denote by OUT _ R^* instead of b_ com . Decommit Stage: C generates a sequence of decommitments decom =( decom _1,..., decom _n) from ST _C . We denote this procedure by decom gets C( ST _C) . Then it sends a sequence of messages vb m =(m_1,...,m_n) and the sequence of decommitments decom =( decom _1,..., decom _n) to R . For each i ∈ [n] , R runs a deterministic verification procedure b_ dec ,i gets Verify _i(τ,m_i, decom _i) where b_ dec ,i =top and b_ dec ,i =bot indicate acceptance and rejection on the i -th bit, respectively. W.l.o.g., we assume that R always rejects (i.e., Verify _i(τ, · , · ) = bot for all i ∈ [n] ) whenever b_ com = bot . (Note that w.l.o.g., τ can include b_ com because we can always modify the protocol to ask R to send b_ com as the last round message.) The scheme satisfies the following requirements: (Completeness.) title: (Strong) Exponential Time Hypothesis
statement_text: Let c_k be the smallest constant such that there is an algorithm for k -CNF SAT that runs in 2^ c_k n +o(n) time. Let r_k be the smallest constant such that there is a randomized algorithm for k -CNF SAT that runs in 2^ r_k n +o(n) time. The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) states that c_k>0 for all k ≥ 3 . The Random ETH (rETH) states that r_k>0 for all k ≥ 3 . The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) states that there is no constant ε>0 such that c_k ≤ 1-ε for all constant k .

label: def:kOV
statement_text: [The k -OV Hypothesis ] In the k - OV problem , we are given k lists L_1, ... , L_k of n zero-one vectors of length d as input. If there are k vectors v_1 ∈ L_1, ... ,v_k ∈ L_k such that for ∀ i ∈ [1,d] ∃ j ∈ [1,k] such that v_i[j]=0 we call these k vectors an orthogonal k -tuple. The output of k - OV is true if there is an orthogonal k -tuple in the input and false otherwise. The counting version of k -OV asks for the number of orthogonal k -tuples. The k - OV hypothesis states that that the k - OV problem requires n^ k-o(1) time, even for randomized algorithms .

label: def:randomnoise
statement_text: Random Noise Corruption Suppose f_n:Σ^ p(n) → D Here, we allow Σ to be any constant length alphabet, and D is any set. The variable n is the growing instance size parameter and p: N → N is a polynomial of constant degree. is the part of the function f of input length parameter n and let T _ f_n denote its truth table on instances of size parameter n (length p(n) ) We use the phrase ``truth table'' even if D is not { 0,1 } , simply out of convention. When we say the truth table, we always refer to the table of all evaluations. . We define N _ δ : D ^ |Σ |^ p(n) → D ^ |Σ |^ p(n) as a random noise operator that acts as follows, acting on T _ f_n as N _ δ T _ f_n - a subset S ⊂ Σ^ p(n) of size δ|Σ|^ p(n) is chosen uniformly at random. A corrupted truth table T _ f_n ^ prime is produced by modifying all entries in S in any possible way, with no restrictions on how they are changed These changes may be adversarial, may be made to minimize the time complexity of computing the function represented by T ^ prime _ f , or to fit any other criterion. , leaving all other entries unchanged.

paper_title: Recovery Reductions, Conjectures, and Barriers
label: def:reduction
statement_text: Recovery Reductions in the Random Noise Model For a given function f:Σ^ * → D , a (t(n), δ, ε ) -recovery reduction in the random noise model is a randomized algorithm A , defined as follows: The random noise operator N _ δ is applied on T _ f_n to produce a corrupted truth table T _ f_n ^ prime . It is unknown to the algorithm which answers are corrupted. With probability 1-ε over the randomness of choice of corruptions, A , given oracle access to the δ -fraction corrupted truth table T ^ prime _ f_n , computes f_n(x) correctly in O (t(n) ) time with probability at least 2/3 .

label: def:semilattice
statement_text: Semilattice A semilattice ( D , odot ) is a set D and a binary operation odot : D × D → D such that: (Associativity) For every x, y, z ∈ D , ( x odot y ) odot z = x odot ( y odot z ) . (Commutativity) For every x, y ∈ D , x odot y = y odot x . (Idempotence) For every d ∈ D , d odot d = d .

paper_title: Recovery Reductions, Conjectures, and Barriers
label: def:computableSL

paper_title: Recovery Reductions, Conjectures, and Barriers
label: def:aggregrate
statement_text: Semilattice NP Semilattice NP ( SLNP ) is the class of functions defined as follows. A function f is in the class SLNP if: There is a polynomial p: N → N and a polynomial-time computable semilattice ( D , odot ) such that for every natural number n , the function f_n:Σ^ p(n) → D is the function f restricted to inputs of size parameter n on a constant sized alphabet Σ . There exists a function h_n:Σ^ p(n) × C _n → D such that f_n(φ) = odot_ x ∈ C _n h_n(φ, x), where |x| = poly (n) , C _n = Π^ poly (n) for some constant- sized alphabet Π and h_n(φ, x) can be computed in time polynomial in n .

For each group G_n , there exist group actions α: G_n × Σ^ p(n) → Σ^ p(n) ( p is the size function associated with the function f ) and β: G_n × C _n → C _n such that: For every φ ∈ Σ^ p(n) , x ∈ C _n , and g ∈ G_n , we have that h_n (α_ g (φ), β_ g (x) ) = h_n (φ, x ). The group action β partitions the set (the certificate space) C _n into j(n) = poly (n) distinct orbits C ^ β _ n, 1 , C ^ β _ n, 2 , ... , C ^ β _ n, j(n) . In poly (n) time, it is possible to compute a list (x_1, x_2, ... , x_ j(n) ) ∈ C _n^ j(n) such that for each i ∈ [j(n) ] , x_ i ∈ C ^ β _ n, i . Now, for every ℓ ∈ [d] , we write the operation E _ ℓ that for all u = (j_1, ... , j_ ℓ -1 ) in the ( ℓ -1) th layer of T acts for all j ∈ [k] , E _ ℓ : |j_1, ... ,j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |j ⟩ |bot ⟩ ^ ⊗ (d- ℓ ) mapsto |j_1, ... ,j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |j ⟩ |bot ⟩ ^ ⊗ (d- ℓ ) , & if u is the root of a tree decomposition , |j_1, ... ,j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |j ⟩ frac |f_ u,j ⟩ | |f_ u,j ⟩ | , & otherwise . Similarly, for all ℓ ∈ [d] , we write U_ ℓ as the operation that for all u = (j_1, ... , j_ ℓ -1 ) in the ( ℓ -1) th layer of T acts as U_ ℓ : |j_1, ... ,j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |bot ⟩ |bot ⟩ ^ ⊗ (d- ℓ ) mapsto |j_1, ... ,j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |bot ⟩ |bot ⟩ ^ ⊗ (d- ℓ ) , & if u is the root of a tree decomposition , |j_1, ... , j_ ℓ -1 ⟩ |ψ_u ⟩ |bot ⟩ ^ ⊗ (d- ℓ ) , & otherwise . Then, we can implement the reflection through C _ G,r in the circuit model with two calls to all the E _ ℓ 's and U_ ℓ 's, and O (d log (K)) auxiliary elementary gates.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:circulation-space-reflection-implementation
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a graph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 , and let T be a tree-parallel decomposition of G , with depth d . For every ℓ ∈ [d] , let k_ ℓ be the maximum number of children nodes of vertices in the ( ℓ -1) th vertex layer, and let K = (k_1 + 1) ... (k_d + 1) . Then, we can implement R_ C _ G,r in the QROM-model with O (|E|K) ⊆ O (|E|^ d+1 ) bits of QROM, and O (d log (K)) ⊆ O (d^2 log |E|) elementary gates.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected multigraph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 , and s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t . Let D ⊆ {0,1}^n and for all e ∈ E , let j(e) ∈ [n] and b(e) ∈ {0,1} . We refer to G = (G,j,b,r) as an st -connectivity graph on D , and we say that it computes the function f : D → {0,1} , where f(x) = 1 if and only if s and t are connected along the graph G(x) = (V,E(x)) , where E(x) = {e ∈ E : x_ j(e) = b(e)} . We let w_+(x, G ) = R_ G(x),s,t,r , and w_-(x, G ) = R_ G,s,t,r' ^ -1 , where r'(e) = r(e)^ -1 if x_ j(e) ≠ b(e) , and 0 otherwise. We say that the complexity of G is C( G ) = sqrt max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) w_+(x, G ) · max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) w_-(x, G ) . Finally, for any boolean function f : D → {0,1} with D ⊆ {0,1}^n , we write st (f) for the minimal complexity C( G ) of an st -connectivity graph G that computes f .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:st-connectivity
statement_text: Let n ∈ N and D ⊆ {0,1}^n . Every st -connectivity graph G = (G,j,e,r) on D can be turned into a graph composition P on D , such that C( P ) = C( G ) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: lem:planar-dual-circulation-space
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a connected, undirected, planar graph, where every edge e ∈ E has an implicit direction meaning that it goes from e_- to e_+ . Let G^ † = (F^ † ,E^ † ) be a planar dual of G , where every edge e is associated to a dual edge e^ † ∈ E^ † , that points from the face on the left of e to the face on the right of e , as seen from the perspective of traversing e in its implicit direction. Moreover, let r : E → [0, ∞ ] be resistances on G , and let r^ † : E^ † → [0, ∞ ] be defined by r^ † _ e^ † = 1/r_e . Then, by identifying |e^ † ⟩ = |e ⟩ , and as such identifying H _ G^ † = H _G , we find that H _G = C _ G,r ⊕ C _ G^ † ,r^ † = H _ G^ † .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:dual-graph-composition
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a connected, undirected graph with s,t ∈ V and s ≠ t , such that G ∪ {(s,t)} is planar. Let G^ † = (F^ † ,E^ † ) be a planar dual of G ∪ {(s,t)} with the dual edge of (s,t) , connecting s^ † and t^ † , removed. For all e ∈ E we denote its dual edge by e^ † , we let P be the span program formed by taking the graph composition of G with the span programs ( P _e)_ e ∈ E , and we let P ^ † be the graph composition of G^ † with span programs ( ¬ P _e)_ e^ † ∈ E^ † . Then, ¬ P = P ^ † .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: def:logical-compositions
title: AND- and OR-composition
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on D . We define two special types of graph compositions: Let G be a line graph with n edges, and let s and t be the endpoints. We let P be the graph composition of G with span programs P _1, ... , P _n on the edges, and we write P = wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j . We refer to this as the AND-composition of P _1, ... , P _n . Let G be a graph with 2 nodes, s and t , and n parallel edges between them. We let P be the graph composition with span programs P _1, ... , P _n on the edges, and we write P = vee_ j=1 ^n P _j . We refer to this construction as the OR-composition of P _1, ... , P _n .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:and-or-witness-sizes
title: Witness sizes of AND- and OR-composition
statement_text: Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on a common domain D . Then, for all x ∈ D , we have w_+ (x, wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = Σ _ j=1 ^n w_+(x, P _j), and w_- (x, wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = [ Σ _ j=1 ^n frac 1 w_-(x, P _j) ]^ -1 , and w_+ (x, vee_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = [ Σ _ j=1 ^n frac 1 w_+(x, P _j) ]^ -1 , and w_- (x, vee_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = Σ _ j=1 ^n w_-(x, P _j).

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: Variable-time search
statement_text: Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on a common domain D . Then, P = vee_ j=1 ^n frac P _j W_+( P _j) ⇒ C ( P )^2 ≤ Σ _ j=1 ^n C( P _j)^2.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:variable-time-formula-evaluation
title: Variable-time formula evaluation
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and φ : D → {0,1} be a boolean formula. Let J(φ) be the multiset of the indices being queried by φ , e.g., J((x_ j_1 ∧ x_ j_2 ) ∨ ( ¬ x_ j_1 ∧ ¬ x_ j_2 )) = {j_1,j_2,j_1,j_2} . Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on D , such that P _j computes the j th bit of x ∈ D . Then we can build a graph composition P on D of a series-parallel graph G that computes φ with complexity C( P )^2 ≤ Σ _ j ∈ J(φ) C( P _j)^2. Moreover, in the QROM-model, we can implement the reflection through the circulation space using a QROM with O (|J(φ)|^ d+1 ) bits, and with O (d^2 log |J(φ)| ) elementary gates, where d is the depth of the AND-OR-tree representation of φ .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: def:divide-and-conquer
title: Quantum divide and conquer,
statement_text: Let a,b,n ∈ N , Σ a finite alphabet, and Λ a finite parameter space. For all m ∈ N and λ ∈ Λ , let f_m^ λ : Σ^n → {0,1} , f_m^ λ, aux : Σ^n → {0,1} , m_1, ... , m_a ∈ Θ(m/b) , λ_1, ... , λ_a ∈ Λ , and φ_m^ λ : {0,1}^ a+1 → {0,1} be a boolean read-once formula, i.e., where each variable appears exactly once, such that there exists a m_0 ∈ N , such that for all m ≥ m_0 and x ∈ Σ^n , f_m^ λ (x) = φ_m^ λ (f_ m_1 ^ λ_1 (x), ... , f_ m_a ^ λ_a (x), f_m^ λ, aux (x)). This defines a quantum divide and conquer strategy for {f_m^ λ }_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:divide-and-conquer
statement_text: Consider a quantum divide and conquer strategy for a family of functions {f_m^ λ }_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ , in the sense of . For all m ∈ N , let P _m^ λ, aux be a span program that evaluates f_m^ λ, aux , and for all m < m_0 , let P _m^ λ be a span program evaluating f_m^ λ . Now, we can build a family of graph compositions ( P _m^ λ )_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ , where for all m ≥ m_0 , P _m^ λ evaluates f_m^ λ , and satisfies C( P _m^ λ )^2 ≤ Σ _ j=1 ^a C( P _ m_j ^ λ_j )^2 + C( P _m^ λ, aux )^2. Moreover, in the QROM-model, the complexity of implementing the reflection through the circulation space, in the graph composition for P _m^ λ , can be done with a QROM of size O ( poly (a^ log (m)/ log (b) )) and using O (( log (m)/ log (b))^2 log (a)) elementary gates.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:savitch
statement_text: There is an st -connectivity algorithm that solves the directed st -connectivity problem making O( sqrt 2n ^ log (n) ) queries, with O ( sqrt 2n ^ log (n) ) elementary gates, and using O( log ^2(n)) space.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: Extended learning graphs
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . We need the following ingredients: A directed acyclic graph G = (V,E) . Labels S : V → 2^ [n] , such that: There is a unique r(G) ∈ V with S(r(G)) = varnothing . For all (u,v) = e ∈ E , there exists a j ∈ [n] such that j ∉ S(u) and S(v) = S(u) ∪ {j} . A weight function w : D × E × {0,1} → R _ ≥ 0 , such that for all (u,v) = e ∈ E , j ∈ [n] such that S(v) = S(u) ∪ {j} and b ∈ {0,1} : For all x,y ∈ D , we have x_ S(v) = y_ S(v) implies w(x,e,b) = w(y,e,b) . For all (x,y) ∈ f^ -1 (1) × f^ -1 (0) , x_ S(u) = y_ S(u) and x_j ≠ y_j implies w(x,e,0) = w(y,e,1) . Finally, for all y ∈ f^ -1 (1) , let p_y : E → R _ ≥ 0 be a unit flow on G , with: A single source node r(G) . The sink nodes are all the nodes v ∈ V for which S(v) contains a 1 -certificate for y . for all e ∈ E , w(y,e,1) = 0 implies p_y(e) = 0 . Then L = (G,S,w,{p_y}_ y ∈ f^ -1 (1) ) is an adaptive learning graph that computes f . For all x ∈ f^ -1 (0) and y ∈ f^ -1 (1) , respectively, we define ℓ _-(x,L) = Σ _ e ∈ E w(x,e,0), and ℓ _+(x,L) = Σ _ e ∈ E (p_y(e)^2)/(w(y,e,1)), and we define L _-(L) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) ℓ _-(x,L), L _+(L) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) ℓ _+(x,L), and L (L) = sqrt L _-(L) · L _+(L) . Finally, we write XLG (f) as the minimum of L (L) over all adaptive learning graphs L that compute f .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:extended-learning-graphs
statement_text: Let L be an extended learning graph. Then, we can construct an instance of the st -connectivity framework that evaluates the learning graph, with complexity at most L (L) . As such, for all f : {0,1}^n ⊇ D → {0,1} , st (f) ≤ L (f) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: Decision tree + guessing algorithm complexity
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree computing f , and let G : E → {0,1} be a guessing algorithm, such that for every internal node v ∈ V , exactly one of its children is connected with an edge e ∈ E for which G(e) = 1 . Then, we write T (T) for the depth of T , and the G (T) for the maximum number of edges e ∈ E along a path from the root to a leaf that satisfy G(e) = 0 . We call G (T) the guessing complexity of T . Finally, we write sqrt GT (f) = min _ T computing f sqrt G (T) · T (T) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: def:weighted-decision-tree
title: Weighted-decision-tree complexity
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree computing f , and w : E → R _ ≥ 0 a weight functions on the edges. For every input x ∈ D , let P _x be the path taken on input x , and let P _x be the set of edges that have exactly one node in common with the vertices traversed in P _x . Then, we define WDT _+( T ,w) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) Σ _ e ∈ P _x w_e, WDT _-( T ,w) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) Σ _ e ∈ P _x (1)/(w_e), and WDT ( T ,w) = sqrt WDT _+( T ,w) · WDT _-( T ,w) . Moreover, we let WDT ( T ) = min _ w : E → R _ ≥ 0 WDT ( T ,w), and WDT (f) = min _ T computing f WDT ( T ).

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: def:zero-error
title: Zero-error version of the complexity measures
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = {T_1, ... , T_k} be a set of decision trees, where every leaf is labeled with 0 , 1 , or ? . Let p= (p_1, ... , p_k) be a probability distribution on [k] , such that for all x ∈ D , if we sample T_j with j p , then the probability that it outputs ¬ f(x) is 0 , and the probability that it outputs ? is at most 1/2 . Then, we say that T computes f with zero error, and we write sqrt GT ( T ) = max _ j ∈ [k] sqrt G (T_j) · T (T_j) , and sqrt GT _0(f) = min _ T computes f with zero error sqrt GT ( T ). and WDT ( T ) = max _ j ∈ [k] WDT (T_j), and WDT _0(f) = min _ T computes f with zero error WDT ( T ).

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:weighted-decision-trees
statement_text: Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree, making queries to an n -bit string, having outputs in {0,1, ? } , and with a weight function w : E → R _ >0 on the edges. Then, we can construct an instance of the st -connectivity framework that distinguishes whether the output of the tree is 1 or an element of {0, ? } with complexity at most WDT ( T ,w) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:st-to-WDT0
statement_text: Let f : D → {0,1} with D ⊆ {0,1}^n . We have st (f) ≤ sqrt 2 WDT _0(f) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:phase-estimation-algo
statement_text: Every span program, evaluated on an input x , is also a phase estimation algorithm, and the span program's positive and negative witnesses are negative and positive witnesses of the phase estimation algorithm, respectively.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:subspace-graph
statement_text: Every graph composition can be turned into a subspace graph with at most the same witness sizes.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:threshold
title: Threshold functions through the st -connectivity framework
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and k ∈ {1, ... , n} . Let f_n^k be the threshold function on n bits with threshold k , i.e., f_n^k(x) = 1 if and only if |x| ≥ k . Let x_j be a trivial span program computing the j th bit of the input. Then, for all S ⊆ [n] , we recursively define Th _ S ^ k+1 = vee_ j ∈ S (x_j ∧ k Th _ S \ {j} ^k), and Th _ S ^1 = vee_ j ∈ S x_j. Then, Th _n^k := Th _ [n] ^k computes f_n^k , with witness sizes w_+(x, Th _n^k) = (1)/(|x|-k+1), & if |x| ≥ k, ∞ , & otherwise , and w_-(x, Th _n^k) = ∞ , & if |x| ≥ k, (k(n-k+1))/(k-|x|), & otherwise . Consequently, C( Th _n^k) = sqrt k(n+k-1) , and this is optimal.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:exact-weight
title: Graph-composition for the exact-weight function
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , k ∈ {1, ... , n-1} , and let f_n^k be the exact-weight function on n bits with weight k , i.e., f_n^k(x) = 1 if and only if |x| = k . We let EW _n^k = k(n+k-1) Th _n^k ∧ ¬ Th _n^ k+1 . Then, EW _n^k computes f_n^k , with witness sizes w_+(x, EW _n^k) = n + 2k(n-k), & if |x| = k, ∞ , & otherwise , and w_-(x, EW _n^k) = ∞ , & if |x| = k, (1)/(|k-|x||), & otherwise . Consequently, C( EW _n^k) = sqrt n + 2k(n-k) , and this is optimal.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: lem:gapped-majority
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D = {x ∈ {0,1}^n : |x| < n/3 ∨ |x| > 2n/3} , and f_n : D → {0,1} be defined as f_n(x) = 1 if and only if |x| > 2n/3 . That is, f_n is the gapped majority function on n inputs. Then, st (f_n) ∈ O(1) , and R _0(f_n) ∈ Ω(n) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:st-vs-R
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n and f : D → {0,1} . Then, st (f) ∈ O( R (f)) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:weighted-decision-tree-complexity
statement_text: Let f : D → {0,1} with D ⊆ {0,1}^n . Then D (f) ≤ WDT (f)^2 .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: cor:R0-WDT02
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . Then, R _0(f) ≤ WDT _0(f)^2 .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:GT-ub-WDT
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . Then, sqrt GT (f) ≤ WDT (f)^ 3/2 and sqrt GT _0(f) ≤ WDT _0(f)^ 3/2 .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:GT-sep-WDT
statement_text: Let n ∈ N and f : {0,1}^ 2n+1 → {0,1} be defined as f(x) = x_2 ⊕ x_3 ⊕ ... ⊕ x_ n+1 , & if x_1 = 1, x_2 ∨ x_3 ∨ ... ∨ x_ n^2+1 , & if x_1 = 0. . Then, WDT (f) ∈ O(n) and sqrt GT _0(f) ∈ Ω(n^ 3/2 ) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: lem:deterministic-sample
title: Deterministic sample
statement_text: Let Σ a finite alphabet of constant size, m,n ∈ N and y ∈ Σ^m aperiodic, i.e., there does not exist a p ≤ m/2 such that y_ kp+ ℓ = y_ ℓ for all ℓ ∈ [p] and 0 ≤ k ≤ lfloor (n- ℓ )/prfloor . Then, there exists a subset J ⊆ [m] and integer 0 ≤ k ≤ m/2 such that |J| ≤ log (m) , and such that if x[j:j+m-1] agrees with y on J , with j ∈ [n-m+1] , then for any non-zero integer max {0,-k} ≤ ℓ ≤ min {m/2-k,n-m+1} , x[j+ ℓ :j+m-1+ ℓ ] does not agree with y .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:aperiodic-pattern-matching
title: Quantum algorithm for aperiodic pattern matching
statement_text: Let Σ be a finite alphabet of constant size, and y ∈ Σ^m an aperiodic pattern. We can solve the aperiodic pattern matching problem with O( sqrt n log (m) ) queries to the input string x ∈ Σ^n , O ( sqrt n ) elementary gates, and a QROM of size O(m) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:pattern-matching
title: Quantum algorithm for pattern matching
statement_text: Let Σ be a finite alphabet of constant size, n,m ∈ N and y ∈ Σ^m be a periodic pattern with period p , and k = lceil m/prceil ≥ 2 (partial) repetitions. Then, we can solve the pattern matching problem with O( sqrt n log (p) ) queries to the input string x ∈ Σ^n .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: The OR ∘ pSEARCH -problem
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and let D _n ⊆ {0,1,*}^n , such that x ∈ D _n if and only if x has exactly one position j(x) ∈ [n] for which x_ j(x) ≠ * . The pSEARCH -problem asks to output the value of x_ j(x) , given query access to x . Next, let m ∈ N , T ∈ {m,m+1, ... ,nm} and let D _T ⊆ D _n^m , such that (x^ (1) , ... , x^ (m) ) ∈ D _T if and only if j(x^ (1) ) + ... + j(x^ (m) ) = T and | x | ∈ {0,1} , where x = x^ (1) _ j(x^ (1) ) ... x^ (m) _ j(x^ (m) ) ∈ {0,1}^m. The OR ∘ pSEARCH -problem asks to output | x | , given query-access to x ∈ D _T .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:or-psearch
statement_text: There is a quantum algorithm that solves the OR ∘ pSEARCH -problem with O( sqrt T log (T) ) queries, which is tight up to constants, O ( sqrt T ) elementary gates, and a QROM of size O (T) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: The Σ^*20^*2Σ^* -problem
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , Σ = {0,1,2} and x ∈ Σ^n . The Σ^*20^*2Σ^* -problem asks whether x is recognized by the regular language Σ^*20^*2Σ^* , i.e., whether there exist j_1,j_2 ∈ [n] such that j_1 < j_2 , x_ j_1 = x_ j_2 = 2 , and x_k = 0 for all k ∈ {j_1+1, ... , j_2-1} .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: thm:202
statement_text: There is a quantum algorithm that evaluates the Σ^*20^*2Σ^* -problem using O( sqrt n log (n) ) queries, and it can be implemented in time O ( sqrt n ) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
title: Bounded-depth Dyck language recognition problem
statement_text: Let k ∈ N , and Σ = { ( , ) } . For any finite string x ∈ Σ^* , we define w(x) = |x^ -1 ( ( )| - |x^ -1 ( ) )| , i.e., the difference of the number of opening and closing brackets in x . The Dyck language of depth k contains all words x ∈ Σ^* , for which w(x) = 0 , and any prefix x' (i.e., any substring at the start of x ) satisfies 0 ≤ w(x') ≤ k . For any even n ∈ N , the depth- k Dyck language recognition problem now asks to determine for a length- n input x ∈ Σ^n , whether it is in the depth- k Dyck language, given query-access to x .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_text: There exists a graph composition algorithm for recognizing the Dyck language of depths 1 and 2 , making O( sqrt n ) queries and spending O ( sqrt n ) time.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
label: lem:dyck3-properties
statement_text: Let n ∈ N even, and x ∈ Σ^n . There is a j ∈ [n] such that j is even, x_j = ( , and for all k ∈ {j+1, ... , n} , x_k = ( if and only if k is odd. We define the Bohr set Λ = Λ_ Θ,ε = cap_ i=1 ^ d {x ∈ G: ‖ Θ_i(x) ‖ _ R / Z ≤ ε }, where |x|_ R / Z = min _ z ∈ Z |x-z| . For any real number c>0 , we define the dilated Bohr set cΛ_ Θ,ε = Λ_ Θ,cε .

paper_title: Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem
label: def:reg-Bohr
title: Regular
statement_text: A Bohr set Λ = Λ_ Θ,ε of dimension d is regular if for all |c| ≤ 1/(100d) , we have that 1 - 100d|c| ≤ (|(1+c)Λ|)/(|Λ|) ≤ 1 + 100d|c|.

paper_title: Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem

paper_title: Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem
label: def:etasmall

statement_text: We say that B_1, B_2, ... is a (d, η) -small sequence of Bohr sets if all B_i have the same set of d frequencies (so that rank (B_i) = d ), are all regular, and ν(B_ i+1 )/ν(B_i) ≤ η for i = 1, 2, ... . We say that the sequence is (d, η) -exact if additionally ν(B_ i+1 )/ν(B_i) ∈ [η/2, η] for all i = 1, 2, ... .

paper_title: Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem
label: def:gow-high

statement_text: Fix integers k, ℓ ≥ 1 . Consider a triplet of Bohr sets B_1 , B_2 , and B_3 and a function f:G → R . We define the (B_1, B_2, B_3, k, ℓ ) -Gowers grid norm to be lVertf ‖ _ (B_1,B_2,B_3, k, ℓ ) ^ k ℓ = mathop E _ substack x B_1 y_1, ... ,y_k B_2 z_1, ... ,z_ ℓ B_3 Π _ substack i ∈ [k] j ∈ [ ℓ ] f(x+y_i+z_j). paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
title: Catalytic space
statement_text: A catalytic Turing Machine with free space s := s(n) and catalytic space c := c(n) is a Turing machine with the following tapes: a read-only input tape of length n which is initialized to x ∈ {0,1}^n a read-write work tape of length s which is initialized to 0^ s a read-write catalytic tape of length c ≤ 2^s which is initialized to some τ ∈ {0,1}^ c

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: def:cspace-variants
title: Variants of catalytic space
statement_text: For a boolean function f , we say a catalytic machine computes f if (deterministic machine) for every x , the machine outputs f(x) . (non-deterministic machine) for every x , if f(x)=1 then there is a sequence on non-deterministic choices where the machine accepts x , and if f(x)=0 then for any sequence on non-deterministic choices the machine rejects. A co-non-deterministic machine must always accept when f(x)=1 and sometimes reject when f(x)=0 . (bounded-error randomized machine) for every x , the machine outputs f(x) with probability at least 2/3 over its random choices. (unbounded-error randomized machine) for every x , the machine outputs f(x) with probability greater than 1/2 over its random choices.

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
title: Complexity classes
statement_text: A catalytic Turing machine decides a language L if it computes the characteristic function of L . For s := s(n) and c := c(n) we define CSPACE [s,c] to be the class of languages which can be computed by a catalytic Turing machine with free space s and catalytic space c . CNSPACE [s,c] ( coCNSPACE [s,c] ) to be the class of languages which can be computed (co-computed) by a non-deterministic catalytic Turing machine with free space s and catalytic space c . CBPSPACE [s,c] to be the class of languages which can be computed by a bounded-error randomized catalytic Turing machine with free space s and catalytic space c . CPSPACE [s,c] to be the class of languages which can be computed by an unbounded-error randomized catalytic Turing machine with free space s and catalytic space c .

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
statement_text: Let M be a catalytic machine with work space s and catalytic space c . We denote by ⟨ π,u ⟩ the configuration of M where π ∈ {0,1}^c is contained on the catalytic tape and u ∈ {0,1}^s is on its work tape.

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: definition_config_graphs
title: Configuration graphs
statement_text: The configuration graph G _ M,x is the directed acyclic graph where each node corresponds to a configuration of M on input x , where there is a directed edge from ⟨ π,u ⟩ to ⟨ π',u' ⟩ iff ⟨ π',u' ⟩ can be reached from ⟨ π,u ⟩ in one execution step of M . The out-degree of every vertex in G _ M,x is at most 2, and there is some fixed constant d_M depending only on M such that each vertex in G _ M,x has in-degree at most d_M-2 . We call the outgoing edges forward edges of ⟨ τ,v ⟩ . The remaining edges of ⟨ τ,v ⟩ are backward edges. A halting configuration has no forward edges in G _ M,x . We say an edge (v,v') is labeled with b ∈ {0,1} if it corresponds to a non-deterministic/randomized b -choice of the machine. For deterministic transitions we label the edge with both 0 and 1 . For every catalytic tape τ let G _ M,x,τ be the subgraph of G _ M,x induced on configurations of G _ M,x that are reachable from start _ M,x,τ . Clearly G _ M,x,τ has one source node, namely start _ M,x,τ , and up to two sink nodes, namely acc _ M,x,τ and rej _ M,x,τ .

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
title: 0 -graph of configuration graphs
statement_text: Given a configuration graph G _ M,x , we let the 0 -graph G ^0_ M,x be the undirected graph where only edges with label 0 are retained, and we forget the direction of each edge. Observe that for every τ and v ∈ G _ M,x,τ , G ^0_ M,x (v) is a tree as each node has at most one forward edge corresponding to the edge labeled 0 in G _ M,x . Given a configuration v , we let G ^0_ M,x (v) be the connected component of G ^0_ M,x containing v .

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
statement_text: Let v, v' be such that v ∈ G ^0_ M,x (v') . Then G ^0_ M,x (v) = G ^0_ M,x (v') and hence v' ∈ G ^0_ M,x (v) .

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
statement_text: Each tree in G ^0_ M,x contains at most one halting configuration.

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: prop:disjointDFS
statement_text: Let τ ≠ τ' ∈ {0,1}^c be two distinct contents of the catalytic tape of a catalytic machine M on an input x . The vertex sets of G ^0_ M,x ( acc _ M,x,τ ) , G ^0_ M,x ( acc _ M,x,τ' ) , G ^0_ M,x ( rej _ M,x,τ ) and G ^0_ M,x ( rej _ M,x,τ' ) are pairwise disjoint.

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: prop:sizeexpectation
statement_text: Let M be a catalytic machine with work space s := s(n) and catalytic space c := c(n) , where log n ≤ s ≤ c ≤ 2^s . Then E _ τ ∈ {0,1}^c [ |V( G ^0_ M,x ( acc _ M,x,τ ))|] ≤ 2^s and E _ τ ∈ {0,1}^c [ |V( G ^0_ M,x ( rej _ M,x,τ ))|] ≤ 2^s.

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: lem:reachInDFS
statement_text: Let M be a valid catalytic machine, and let ⟨ π,u ⟩ be an arbitrary node in G _ M,x,τ . Then, ⟨ π,u ⟩ ∈ V( G ^0_ M,x ( acc _ M,x,τ )) ∪ V( G ^0_ M,x ( rej _ M,x,τ )) .

paper_title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
label: lemma:compressorcompute
statement_text: Let M be a catalytic machine with work space s := s(n) and catalytic space c := c(n) , where log n ≤ s ≤ c ≤ 2^s , and let x ∈ {0,1}^n be an input for M written on the input tape. Let B= 2s and S=2^B , and let τ ∈ {0,1}^c and tar ∈ {0,1}^B be given on the catalytic tape. There is a catalytic subroutine ComputeOrCompress (τ, tar ) which takes one of the following two actions: If both G ^0_ M,x ( acc _ M,x,τ ) and G ^0_ M,x ( rej _ M,x,τ ) are of size at most S/2+1 , then it outputs a directed graph G and two vertices r and t such that the forward reachable graph from r is isomorphic to G _ M,x,τ , with start _ M,x,τ mapping to r and acc _ M,x,τ mapping to t . Otherwise, it replaces τ by π ∈ {0,1}^c and tar by (u,j,0^ s- log d_M ) , where u ∈ {0,1}^s and j ∈ [d_M] have the property that CountStepsBack ( ⟨ π,u ⟩ ,j) replaces π by τ and returns tar as the number of steps. The subroutine returns a bit indicating which action it took, and the procedure leaves other portions of the tapes unchanged. Furthermore ComputeOrCompress (τ, tar ) uses additional space O(s) .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Matching
statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph. A matching is a set M ⊆ E of edges such that ∀ v ∈ V, \ |E(v) ∩ M| ≤ 1 A vertex v ∈ V is matched by M (and otherwise unmatched) if |E(v) ∩ M| = 1 The size of the matching M is |M| , and we call a matching perfect if every vertex is matched.

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
statement_text: The matching function , denoted by MATCH , takes as input an n × n bipartite graph G and returns a matching M in G of maximum size.

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Symmetric Difference
statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be a graph. The symmetric difference of matchings M_1, M_2 ⊆ E , denoted by M_1 Δ M_2 , is defined as having edges (M_1 smallsetminus M_2) ∪ (M_2 smallsetminus M_1) . Similarly for any matching M and set S ⊆ E , we define M ⊕ S as (M ∪ S) smallsetminus (M ∩ S) .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Catalytic machines
statement_text: Let s := s(n) and c := c(n) . A catalytic Turing machine with space s and catalytic space c is a Turing machine M with a read-only input tape of length n , a write-only output tape, a read-write work tape of length s , and a second read-write work tape of length c called the catalytic tape , which will be initialized to an adversarial string τ . We say that M computes a function f if for every x ∈ {0,1}^n and τ ∈ {0,1}^c , the result of executing M on input x with initial catalytic tape τ fulfils two properties: 1) M halts with f(x) written on the output tape; and 2) M halts with the catalytic tape in state τ .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Catalytic classes
statement_text: We define CSPACE [s,c] to be the family of functions computable by catalytic Turing machines with space s and catalytic space c . We also define catalytic logspace as CL := cup_ d ∈ N CSPACE [d log n, n^d] Furthermore we define CLP as the family of functions computable by CL machines that are additionally restricted to run in polynomial time for every initial catalytic tape τ .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: lem:DET-in-cl
statement_text: Let N be an n × n matrix over a field of size exp (n) . Then DET (N) is computable in CLP .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: lem:compute-min-weight-path
statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be a directed graph, let s,t ∈ V be a given source and target vertex, and W: E → Z _ ≤ poly (n) be edge weights such that G does not have any non-positive weight cycles under W . Then there exists a CLP machine which, given (G, s, t, W) , computes the minimum weight of a simple s - t path.

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: NC
statement_text: A language L is computable in (uniform) NC if there exists a (uniform) circuit family {C_n}_ n ∈ N such that C_n has size poly (n) , depth log ^ O(1) n , and decides membership in L on all inputs of size n .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Lossy coding and LOSSYC
statement_text: The lossy coding problem is defined as follows: given a pair of algorithms Comp :{0, 1}^n → {0, 1}^ n-1 and Decomp : {0, 1}^ n-1 → {0, 1}^n as input, our goal is to output any x ∈ {0, 1}^n such that Decomp (Comp (x)) ≠ x . Let C be a complexity class. We define LOSSYC as the set of languages reducible to the lossy coding problem whose input algorithms come from the class C . When no class is given, we define LOSSY := LOSSY [ P ] .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
statement_text: Let U be a set and W:U → Z be a weight assignment, and let F ⊆ 2^U be a family of subsets of U . We say that W is isolating for F if ∃ ! \ S_ unique ∈ F such that W(S_ unique ) = min _ F ∈ F W(F) where ∃ ! means that exactly one such set exists.

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: thm:isolated-pm
statement_text: Let G = (V = L ∪ R, E) be a bipartite graph, and let W:E → Z _ ≤ poly (n) be a weight assignment that isolates a perfect matching M_ unique in G . Then there exists an Logspace ^ DET machine which, given input (G, e ∈ E) and access to W , determines whether e ∈ M_ unique .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: lem:isolated-km
statement_text: Let G = (V = L ∪ R, E) be a bipartite graph, and let k ∈ N be a parameter whose value is at most the size of the maximum matching of G . Let W:E → Z _ ≤ poly (n) be edge weights such that W isolates a size k matching M^k_ unique in G . Then there exists a CLP machine which, given input (G, e ∈ E) and access to W , determines whether e ∈ M^k_ unique .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: clique-isolation
statement_text: Let G = (V = L ∪ R, E) be an s × s bipartite clique, and let W:E → Z be weights defined as W(e = (u, v)) = u · v for an arbitrary indexing of V . Then W isolates a perfect matching in G .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Residual Graph
statement_text: Let G = (V = L ∪ R, E) be a bipartite graph, M be a matching in G , and W:E → Z be edge weights. The residual graph of M , which we denote by G^M_ residual = (V^M_ residual , E^M_ residual ) , is a directed graph whose vertex set V^M_ residual consists of V plus a new source s and a new sink t . The edge set E^M_ residual consists of the following edges where u ∈ L and v ∈ R : if u is unmatched by M we add an edge (s → u) , and if v is unmatched by M we add an edge (v → t) if (u,v) ∈ M we add an edge (v → u) if (u,v) ∈ E smallsetminus M we add an edge (u → v) We will drop the M superscript in cases where the usage is clear.

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
title: Augmenting Path
statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be a graph, M be a matching in G , and W:E → Z be a weight assignment. A path P = {e_1, ... , e_m} on vertices {v_1, ... , v_ m+1 } is an augmenting path with respect to M if: v_1 and v_ m+1 are not matched by M . For all odd i ∈ [m] , e_i ∉ M . For all even i ∈ [m] , e_i ∈ M .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
statement_text: Let G = (V = L ∪ R, E) be a bipartite graph, M be a matching in G , and W:E → Z be a weight assignment. We define the alternating weight function as W_ alt ^M(e) vcentcolon = -W(e), & if e ∈ M W(e), & if e ∉ M Furthermore, for residual graph G^M_ residual we define the residual weight function as W_ residual ^M(e) vcentcolon = 0, & if e ∉ E W_ alt ^M(e), & otherwise Whenever we use weights in G^M_ residual , we are referring to the weights W^M_ residual , while for augmenting paths P with respect to M we use W_ alt ^M .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace
label: fact:augmented-matching
title: Berge's Theorem
statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be a graph, M be a matching in G , and W:E → Z be a weight assignment. Then M is maximum iff there do not exist any augmenting paths with respect to M . Furthermore, for any augmenting path P , M ⊕ P is a matching in G of size |M| + 1 .

paper_title: Bipartite Matching is in Catalytic Logspace

statement_text: A streaming algorithm is a sequence of maps m^ (t) and u^ (t) as follows. Let β : {-1} ∪ N → N be a buffer size function with β(-1) = 1 . Denote the state at time t by s^ (t) ∈ R ^ β(t) . Initially, the state is s^ (-1) = 0 ∈ R . Upon receiving z_ t , the algorithm updates its internal state: s^ (t) = u^ (t) (s^ (t-1) , z_ t ), where u^ (t) : R ^ β(t-1) × R → R ^ β(t) . The algorithm then outputs m^ (t) (s^ (t) ) where m^ (t) : R ^ β(t) → R . We assume that the state maps are continuous; for each t , the map (z_0, ... ,z_t) mapsto s^ (t) is assumed to be continuous. The algorithm solves the streaming problem defined by M ∈ R ^ N × N if for every z and every t , m^ (t) (s^ (t) ) = (M z)_t .

paper_title: On the Space Complexity of Online Convolution
statement_text: For time t and a time bound τ ≥ t , define space _M(t;τ) as the minimum value b such that there is a streaming algorithm with buffer size β that computes M correctly up to time τ and b ≥ max _ t' ≤ t β(t') . For infinite streams, the space complexity space _M(t) is defined as space _M(t)= space _M(t; ∞ ) . For a sequence a that defines the Toeplitz matrix T = T[a] , we use the notation space _a(t, τ) coloneqq space _ T[a] (t, τ) .

statement_text: If the algorithm defined by the maps { (u^ (t) , m^ (t) ) : t ∈ N } always outputs a linear function of z , then there is an algorithm that uses only linear maps that computes the same function of z .

paper_title: On the Space Complexity of Online Convolution
statement_text: A polynomial Q(x) of degree d is an expression of the form Q(x) = Σ _ k=0 ^ d q_k x^k where q_d ≠ 0 . The polynomial Q(x) is invertible if q_0 ≠ 0 . The generating function G is a rational function of degree at most d if there are polynomials P,Q with Q invertible so that Q(x) · G(x) = P(x) where deg (Q) ≤ d and deg (P) ≤ d-1 . We say that G has degree d if it is of degree at most d but not of degree at most d-1 . We say that G is irrational if it is not rational (of any degree).

statement_text: Let f: R ^n → R ^k and g : R ^k → R be two polynomial maps. Write f = (f_1, ... ,f_k) , where each f_i : R ^n → R is a polynomial map. paper_title: On the Space Complexity of Online Convolution
title: streaming model with look-ahead
statement_text: The streaming model with look-ahead allows for the algorithm at time t to also query entries in z_ > t and branch on their value. The resulting maps are represented as u ^ (t) : R ^ β(t-1) × R ^ N → R ^ β(t) , m ^ (t) : R ^ β(t) × R ^ N → R , where the state is updated via s ^ (t) = u ^ (t) ( s ^ (t-1) , z_ ≥ t ) where s ^ (-1) = 0 and the algorithm outputs m ^ (t) ( s ^ (t) , z_ >t ) . The map s ^ (t) is assumed continuous as a function in z_ ≤ t (that is, for every fixed z_ >t , the map z_ ≤ t mapsto s ^ (t) (z) is continuous).

Then, the success probability of A is at most 2 · MaxS _ DLOG (T) + (4 log _e(2) ST)/(N) + (T^2)/(N) ≤ (3T^2 )/(N) + (4 log _e(2) ST)/(N).

statement_text: Let A=(A_0,A_1) be a key-recovery, non-adaptive (S,T) -adversary for the Even-Mansour cryptosystem, which can query only the public and encryption oracles and not the decryption oracle. Denote by MaxS _ EM (T) the optimal success probability of a non-preprocessing, non-adaptive algorithm that makes at most T queries. title: Shearer's lemma

statement_text: For a finite set X , let Q=(Q_1,Q_2, ... ,Q_N) be the uniform distribution on X ^N = X × ... × X , and let P=(P_1, ... ,P_N) be another distribution on X ^N . Then k · D_ KL ( P | Q ) ≥ Σ _ j ∈ [m] D_ KL ( P_ U _j | Q_ U _j ), where for U ={i_1, ... i_ ℓ } ⊂ [N] , P_ U =(P_ i_1 , ... ,P_ i_ ℓ ) is the marginal distribution of P on X ^ ℓ , and analogously for Q .

statement_text: A family {f_1,f_2, ... ,f_m} of functions over a product space X ^N is called a read- k family if for each 1 ≤ i ≤ N , at most k of the functions depend on the i 'th coordinate.

statement_text: Let X be a set of size N . statement_text: Let X be a set of size N . Similarly, denote q_j = E _ Q_X [f_j(X)] and q = (1)/(m) · Σ _ j ∈ [m] q_j . Then 2k · D_ KL ( P_X | Q_X ) ≥ m · D_ KL ( p | q ), where D_ KL ( p | q ) = p log ((p)/(q)) + (1-p) log ((1-p)/(1-q)) is the KL-divergence between two Bernoulli distributions with parameters p and q .

label: def:MID
statement_text: A middle game MID has the same setting as PC , and it differs only in the allowed actions for the adversary. An adversary A is a pair of algorithms ( A _0, A _1) that work as follows: A _0 receives only N as input, and outputs constraints which include a pair of sequences I = (I_1, ... ,I_ T_1 ) and O = (O_1, ... ,O_ T_1 ) , each containing non-repeating elements from [N] . Then a permutation σ:[N] → [N] is sampled uniformly from the set of permutations satisfying σ(I_j) = O_j for all j . A _1 is defined similarly to the algorithm A_1 from PC , but with respect to that permutation σ , and it is allowed to make only outer queries and no inner queries . The outer queries of A _1 may depend on I and O . The rest of the game is defined similarly. The running time T_2 of A _1 is defined as the number of queries it makes, and the total running time of A is defined as T := T_1 + T_2 .

paper_title: Non-Adaptive Cryptanalytic Time-Space Lower Bounds via a Shearer-like Inequality for Permutations
label: def:adaptivity
title: Adaptivity ( , Definition 2)
statement_text: We say that an oracle algorithm is k -round adaptive if the algorithm's oracle queries consist of k sets, such that each set of queries depends on the advice string, the input, and the replies to the previous rounds of queries. We call a 1 -round adaptive algorithm non-adaptive. Finally, we say that an algorithm is strongly non-adaptive if it issues a single set of queries that only depends on the algorithm’s input, but not on the advice string. In all of the above cases, when referring to the number of queries made by the algorithm, we account for the sum over all rounds.

statement_text: Let PC := PC (N, D , M , tr , post , suc ) be a permutation challenge game, such that tr is u -uniform and post ( d ,j)=j is a trivial post-processing function. statement_text: An abstract reduction system (ARS) is a pair (A, → ) with a set A and a binary relation → ⊆ A × A . paper_title: Weighted Rewriting: Semiring Semantics for Abstract Reduction Systems
label: def:multiARS
title: Sequence Abstract Reduction System
statement_text: A sequence abstract reduction system (sARS) is a pair (A, → ) consisting of a set A and a binary relation → ⊆ A × Seq (A) . We write a → B = [b_1, b_2, ... ] if B ∈ Seq (A) and (a,B) ∈ → . Normal forms and NF _ → are defined as for ARSs. The sARS (A, → ) is deterministic if for every a ∈ A there is at most one B with a → B and finitely non-deterministic if for each a ∈ A , there are only finitely many B ∈ Seq (A) with a → B . The sARS is finitely branching if for every a → B , the sequence B is finite.

paper_title: Weighted Rewriting: Semiring Semantics for Abstract Reduction Systems
label: def:Reduction Tree
title: Reduction Tree
statement_text: Let (A, → ) be an sARS. An (A, → ) -reduction tree ( (A, → ) -RT) T = (V,E) is a labeled, ordered tree with nodes V and directed edges E ⊆ V × V , where every node v ∈ V is labeled by an object a_v ∈ A and every node v together with its sequence of direct successors vE = [w ∈ V | (v,w) ∈ E] either corresponds to a reduction step a_v → [a_w | w ∈ vE] or vE is empty. We say that (A, → ) is terminating if all (A, → ) -RTs have finite depth. One could instead attempt to define reduction trees in an inductive way. Then every node labeled with a value from A would be a reduction tree and one could lift the reduction → to a binary relation ⇒ which extends reduction trees, i.e., T ⇒ T ' holds if there is a leaf v of T and a reduction step a_v → B such that the reduction tree T ' extends T by new leaves w_b with a_ w_b = b and edges (v,w_b) for all b ∈ B . However, in this way one would only obtain reduction trees of finite depth, whereas we also need reduction trees of infinite depth in order to represent non-terminating reductions, which would require an additional limit step in the construction above.

statement_text: Let S be a semiring and V = { v_1, v_2, ... } be a set of variables. If an aggregator is constructed via finite sequences F , then it is a finite aggregator . Let V (f) be the set of all variables in f ∈ F and let max V (f) = sup {i | v_i ∈ V (f)} ∈ N ^ ∞ . Let f ∈ F and n ∈ N ^ ∞ with n ≥ max V (f) . Then the aggregator f induces a function f: S ^n → S in the obvious way: For a sequence T = [s_1, ... ] ∈ Seq ( S ) of length n , we have s(T) = s for constants s , v_i(T) = s_i for variables v_i and 1 ≤ i ≤ n , and ( circ F)(T) = circ [f_1(T), f_2(T), ... ] for F = [f_1, f_2, ... ] , where circ ∈ { oplus, odot} .

title: Memory Consumption of Operating System
statement_text: Consider a very simplified operating system See for a more involved operating system algorithm that guarantees mutual exclusion. with two processes P_1 and P_2 that should be performed repeatedly. The operating system can either be idle, run a process, or add a process at the end of the waiting queue. We represent this by the ARS ( OS , → ) with OS = { idle (p), wait (p), run (p) | p ∈ {P_1, P_2}^*} . So an object from OS represents the current state of the operating system ( idle , wait , or run ) and the current waiting queue p . The rules of the ARS are idle (p) → wait (p) , idle (p) → run (p) (add a new process to the waiting queue or run some process), wait (p) → idle (p P_1), wait (p) → idle (p P_2) (add P_1 or P_2 to the waiting queue), and run (P_1 p) → idle (p), run (P_2 p) → idle (p) (run the process waiting the longest) for all p ∈ {P_1, P_2}^* . We use the wARS ( OS , → , S _ arc , f _ NF ^ size , Aggr _ a → B ^ size ) with f _ NF ^ size ( run (ε)) = 0 for NF _ → = { run (ε) } and ccccccc Aggr _ idle (p) → wait (p) ^ size &=& Aggr _ idle (p) → run (p) ^ size &=& v_1 Aggr _ run (P_1 p) → idle (p) ^ size &=& Aggr _ run (P_2 p) → idle (p) ^ size &=& v_1 Aggr _ wait (p) → idle (p P_1) ^ size &=& Aggr _ wait (p) → idle (p P_2) ^ size &=& v_1 ⊕ _ S _ arc ( |p| + 1 ) &=& max {v_1,|p| + 1}. Note that we may have a different aggregator for every sequence p ∈ {P_1, P_2}^* , i.e., |p| + 1 is a constant. We obtain llbracket idle (ε) rrbracket ^ _ = ∞ , proving that a reduction leading to a waiting queue of unbounded size exists.

The weight of the tree T from is llbracket T rrbracket ^ _ = nicefrac 4 9 , since nicefrac 4 9 is the probability to reach 0 within two steps. The weight of the infinite extension T _ ∞ of the depicted tree T is llbracket T _ ∞ rrbracket ^ _ = 1 , as such a random walk terminates with probability 1 . In this way one can use semiring semantics to express almost-sure termination (AST) of pARSs . Additionally, consider a certain ``unsafe'' property, e.g., hitting an even number. To analyze whether all infinite sequences are safe, we take the product semiring S = S _ N ^ ∞ × S _ B over S _ N ^ ∞ and the Boolean semiring S _ B . We use the normal form interpretation f _ NF (0) = (0, true ) and the aggregator Aggr _ n mathrel smash stackrel raisebox 2.0pt tiny s smash → [m] = (1,[n mod 2 = 0]) ⊕ _ S v_1 for every n → m . label: ex:starvation-freedom
title: Starvation Freedom
statement_text: To analyze starvation freedom , i.e., whether every process will eventually be served, one can use the tuple semiring S _ N ^ ∞ × S _ N ^ ∞ for our operating system from (a corresponding more complex example for starvation freedom is presented in ). Now the two entries of the tuples count how often a process was already served. Thus, we can use the wARS ( OS , → , S _ N ^ ∞ × S _ N ^ ∞ , f _ NF ^ starv , Aggr _ a → B ^ starv ) with f _ NF ^ starv ( run (ε)) = 0 _ ( S _ N ^ ∞ × S _ N ^ ∞ ) = (0,0) and the aggregator ccccc Aggr _ idle (p) → wait (p) ^ starv &=& Aggr _ idle (p) → run (p) ^ starv &=& v_1 Aggr _ wait (p) → idle (p P_1) ^ starv &=& Aggr _ wait (p) → idle (p P_2) ^ starv &=& v_1 && Aggr _ run (P_1 p) → idle (p) ^ starv &=& (1,0) ⊕ v_1 && Aggr _ run (P_2 p) → idle (p) ^ starv &=& (0,1) ⊕ v_1 However, starvation freedom cannot be analyzed via our current definition of llbracket a rrbracket ^ _ in . We have llbracket a rrbracket ^ _ = ( ∞ , ∞ ) for all a ∈ OS \ { run (ε)} (i.e., for all non-normal forms). This means that for every such start configuration a , there exists a (``worst-case'') reduction of weight ( ∞ , ∞ ) where both processes are served infinitely often. However, for starvation freedom, one [3] would have to show that every infinite reduction serves both processes infinitely often (i.e., this would need to hold irrespective of how the non-determinism in the reductions is resolved). However, ( OS , → ) is not starvation free, since, e.g., we may only serve P_1 infinitely often. So a property like starvation freedom cannot be expressed with our current definition of llbracket a rrbracket ^ _ , because due to the use of the least upper bound in , here we only focus on worst-case reductions. An extension of our approach to also analyze (bounds on) best-case reductions in order to prove properties like starvation freedom is an interesting direction for future work.

statement_text: Let X denote a ground set, and let F be a collection of functions mapping elements from X to the interval [0,1] . statement_text: Let VC be a Vertex Cover of H . M = VC ∪ L'' ∪ {v_*'} is a MEG-set of G. Furthermore, let VC be a Vertex Cover of H with size k . Since VC is a Vertex Cover , at least one of u and v must belong to VC , therefore we assume w.l.o.g.\ that u ∈ VC . Each path from v'' to u must either pass through the vertex v or pass through the vertex v_* . The shortest path including v is ⟨ {v'',v'}, {v',v}, {v,u} ⟩ and has length 3 . Each path passing through v_* must contain at least four edges. Therefore {u,v} is monitored by {v'',u} , where both v'' and u are in M since v'' ∈ L'' and u ∈ VC . Case 2: e ∈ E_ L'' ∪ E_ * . In this case, there is exactly one endpoint u' of e that belongs to L' and either e = {u'', u'} or e = {v_*, u'} . Notice that there is a unique shortest path from v_*' to u'' including the edges {v_*',v_*}{v_*,u'},{u',u''} . This implies that the edge e is monitored by {v'_*, u''} , where both v'_* and u'' ∈ L'' are in M . Case 3: e ∈ E_ L' . Let e = {u,u'} where u is the unique endpoint of e in V(H) . If u ∈ VC then there is a single shortest path from u'' to u and it includes the edge {u,u'} . If u ∉ VC then there exists a neighbor v of u such that v ∈ VC . Similar arguments to those used in Case 1 show that there is a single shortest path from u'' ∈ L'' to v containing the edge {u,u'} . Case 4: e = {v'_*, v_*} . All shortest paths from v'_* to any other vertex in G must traverse e , and hence e is monitored, e.g., by all pairs {v'_*, u} with u ∈ VC . The cardinality |M| is equal to the sum of the cardinality of M \ V(H) and the cardinality of M ∩ V(H) with (M \ V(H)) ∩ (M ∩ V(H)) = ∅ . Since |M ∩ V(H)| is equal to the size k of the Vertex Cover of the graph H and M \ V(H) = L'' ∪ {v_*'} , we can conclude that: |M| = |M ∩ V(H)| + |M \ V(H)| = k + |L''| + |{v_*'}| = k + |V(H)| + 1

label: megToVertexCover
statement_text: Let M be a MEG-set of G with size k + |V(H)| + 1 (for a suitable value of k ). M ∩ V(H) is a Vertex Cover of H with size at most k . Let M'= M \ (L' ∪ {v_*}) be the set obtained by removing the vertex v_* and all the vertices of L' from the MEG-set M . Due to Lemma , M' is a MEG-set of G . Moreover since (L' ∪ {v_*}) ∩ V(H) = ∅ , we can observe that M' ∩ V(H) = M ∩ V(H) . We prove that if {u,v} is an edge of H then at least one of its endpoints is in M' . By contradiction suppose that there exists some {u,v} ∈ E(H) such that neither u nor v are in M' and let {x,y} be a pair of vertices in M' that covers {u,v} . Notice that ∀ u,v ∈ V(G) there exists a path of length at most four that uses only edges in E(G) \ E(H) . This implies that the distance d(x,y) from x to y in G is at most 3 . Moreover d(x,y) ≥ 3 since otherwise we would have {x,y} ∩ {u,v} ≠ ∅ and {x,y} ∩ {u,v} ⊆ M' . The above discussion implies that d(x,y) = 3 and, w.l.o.g., x must be a neighbor of u and y must be a neighbor of v . Let N(u) and N(v) be the set of neighbors of u and v in G , respectively. We have that N(u) ∩ M' ⊆ V(H) (resp N(V) ∩ M' ⊆ V(H) ) since the only neighbor of u (resp v ) that is not in V(H) is u' (resp v' ) but neither u' nor v' belong to M' . Therefore x,y ∈ V(H) and using the fact that the diameter of H is at most 2 , we have d(x,y) ≤ diam (H) ≤ 2 , which contradicts d(x,y) ≥ 3 . The above discussion shows that M' ∩ V(H) is a vertex cover of H . The size of such a vertex cover is |M' ∩ V(H)| ≤ |M ∩ V(H)| = |M| - |M \ V(H)| ≤ |M| - (|V(H)| + 1) = k , where we used (L'' ∪ {v'_*}) ⊆ M \ V(H) , as ensured by Lemma .

label: MegNPComplete
statement_text: The MEG-set decision problem is NP -Complete. For each graph H with diam (H) ≤ 2 it is possible to construct (in polynomial time) a graph G as seen in this section. From Lemmas and we obtain that ∃ Vertex Cover VC of H : |VC| ≤ k ⟺ ∃ MEG-set M of G : |M| ≤ k + |V(H)| + 1 . Since the Vertex Cover problem is NP -Hard even for graphs H with diam (H) ≤ 2 , this implies that the MEG-set decision problem is NP -Hard. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm, MEG-check , that runs in polynomial time and verifies whether M ⊆ V(G) is a MEG-set . As M is a certificate, the MEG-set decision problem is in NP . The algorithm MEG-check takes a graph G and a subset M ⊆ V(G) as input and returns True if and only if M is a MEG-set of the graph G and |M| ≤ k . newpage The MEG-check algorithm, given a graph G and a subset of M ⊆ V(G) of vertices, examines each pair of vertices {x,y} in [M]^2 to determine the edges monitored by this pair. To check if an edge e ∈ E(G) is monitored by a pair {u,v} it suffices to remove the edge e and check if the distance between u and v increases. The correctness of the algorithm stems from the observation that the distance from x to y increases when an edge e ∈ E(G) , monitored by vertices x and y in the subset M , is removed. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that the removal of edge e does not result in an increase in the distance from x to y . This implies the existence of a shortest path between x and y that does not include e . Consequently, e is not monitored by vertices x and y in M . However, this contradicts the assumption that e is monitored by x and y in M . Thus, the algorithm ensures that the removal of monitored edges accurately reflects the changes in the shortest paths between vertices in the subset M . The time complexity of the algorithm can be characterized as: The outer loop iterates over each pair of vertices in [M]^2 , resulting in |[M]^2| = O(|V(G)|^2) iterations. Finding the shortest path P_ xy may involve running a shortest path algorithm that has a time complexity of O(|E(G)|) since the graph is unweighted and connected. The inner loop iterates over the edges in the shortest path from x to y and performs operations inside. Notice that the number of edges contained in this shortest path must be in O(|V(G)|) , because a simple path from x to y contains at most O(|V(G)|) edges. The check performed on the distances requires recalculating a shortest path which has a time complexity of O(|E(G)|) . The last if statement takes O(|E(G)|) time. The time complexity is O(|V(G)|^2 · (|E(G)| + (|V(G)| · |E(G)|))) = O(|V(G)|^3 · |E(G)|) . Then the time complexity is polynomial in the size of the input.

label: thm:aut-on-Ref-Res
statement_text: The following hold for Resolution: Resolution is automatable if, and only if, it is automatable on Ref formulas; Resolution is weakly automatable if, and only if, it is weakly automatable on Ref formulas.

paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
statement_text: For every k ≥ 1 , Res (k) is weakly automatable if, and only if, Res (k) is weakly automatable on Ref formulas.

paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
label: cor:prop-unprovability
title: Propositional unprovability of Resolution lower bounds
statement_text: For every propositional proof system S ≥ Res implicationally simulating Resolution and closed under contrapositions and clause substitutions, if S is not polynomially bounded, there exists a family of unsatisfiable CNF formulas {ψ_n}_ n ∈ N on N = poly (n) variables and of size |ψ_n| = poly (n) such that they require size at least 2^ N^ Ω(1) to be refuted in Resolution; there is a polynomial p(n) such that the formulas { ¬ Ref _ p(n) (ψ_n)}_ n ∈ N are tautological but do not have polynomial-size proofs in S .

paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
label: thm:fo-unprovable
statement_text: Let T be a consistent first-order extending S^1_2 with a set of axioms recognizable in polynomial time and admitting N as a model. Then, there exits a sequence of unsatisfiable propositional formulas { ψ_ k, s }_ k, s ∈ N described uniformly by a polynomial-time algorithm given k and s in unary, where ψ_ k,s has N = poly (k, s) variables, and such that sep=0pt Resolution refutations of the formula ψ_ k, s require size 2^ N^ Ω(1) ; there are constants c >0 and N_0 ∈ N such that the lower bound expressed by the first-order sentence ∀ k ∀ s ∀ π ( N > N_0 ∧ Ref _ Res (ψ_ k, s , π) → |π| > N^ c ) is independent of T .

paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem

statement_text: Let T be a consistent first-order extending Q with a set of axioms recognizable in polynomial time. paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
title: Hypergraph
statement_text: A hypergraph is a pair H = (V, E) of a set V (Vertices), and a family E (edges) of subsets of V . We say H is k -uniform if all edges have size k . Furthermore, we define for a given hypergraph n = |V| and m = |E| .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:transfer_filtration
title: Transfer filtration
statement_text: A hypergraph H=(V,E) is of transfer type b if there exists a chain of subhypergraphs (denoted a transfer filtration of type b ) H_0 ⊆ H_1 ⊆ ... ⊆ H_m=H and an ordering of the edges E(H)={E_1, ... ,E_m} such that E(H_i)={E_1, ... ,E_i} for each i ∈ {0, ... ,m} , |V(H_i)| ≤ |V(H_ i-1 )|+1 for each i ∈ {1, ... ,m} , if |V(H_i)|= |V(H_ i-1 )|+1 , then V(H_i) \ V(H_ i-1 ) ⊆ E_i , |V(H_0)|=b , where we call V(H_0) the foundation , and each edge of H has at least one vertex not in V(H_0) .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:radius:aldi
title: Radius of transfer filtration
statement_text: Let H be a hypergraph admitting a transfer filtration H_0 ⊆ ... ⊆ H_m=H of type b . Consider the function (whose existence is guaranteed according to Remark 16 in ) r:{0, ... ,m} → {0, ... ,m-1} such that r(0)=0 and r(i) is the smallest integer such that |E_i \ V(H_ r(i) )|= 1 for all i ∈ {1, ... ,m} . The radius of the transfer filtration H_0 ⊆ ... ⊆ H_m=H of type b is the smallest integer β such that r^β(i)=0 ∀ i ∈ {1, ... ,m} ( r^β denotes the composition of r with itself β times).

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:core
title: Core
statement_text: Let H=(V, E) be a hypergraph. A core C ⊆ V is any subset causing the following program to output 1 : Remove all edges e ∈ E such that e ⊆ C . While E is non-empty: If there exists e ∈ E such that |e ∩ C| = |e|-1 , set C:=C ∪ e . Else, return 0 . Remove all edges e ∈ E such that e ∩ C=e . Return 1 . Above, any edge, which is removed, is said to have been covered . Any vertex added in step 2(a) is said to be assimilated . We say that an edge is extending if it gets deleted in step 2(a) and non-extending if it gets deleted in step 2(c) . In the following, we refer to this program with the name propagation algorithm .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:radius
title: Radius of the core
statement_text: Let G=(V,E) be a hypergraph with core C . We define the radius r(C) of C as the minimum r , such that E can be subdivided into r disjoint layers L_1, ... ,L_r so that |e ∩ V_ i-1 | = |e| - 1 for all e ∈ L_i , where V_i := C ∪ cup_ j=1 ^ i V(L_j) . We say that a vertex v is in layer i if v ∈ V_i/V_ i-1 .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: lemma:core_eq_transfer-filtration
statement_text: Let H be a hypergraph. H has a transfer filtration H_0 ⊆ H_1 ⊆ ... ⊆ H_m=H of minimum type b with minimal radius k if and only if H has a minimum core C of size b with minimal radius k .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: lemma:edge-oder_degree-one-vertex
statement_text: Let H be a hypergraph. If H has a core of size n-m it has a degree one vertex.

statement_text: Given a hypergraph H = (V,E) , Algorithm outputs a core of size n-m with optimal radius if and only if it exists. The runtime is O(n · m) .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: th:QSAT
statement_text: Let H be a generic PRODSAT instance with constraints in Q [i] on qubits with underlying hypergraph G = ( V, E ) with SDR and a core of size n-m+a with radius r . We can compute an ε -approximate product-state solution in time poly( L , a^r , m^a , | log ε| ), where L is a bound on the bit size of the instance’s rational coefficients, and ε the Euclidean distance to the closest product-state solution.

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: problem:peer_pressure
title: MinCore
statement_text: Given as input a hypergraph H=(V, E) , where hyperedges E are sets of arbitrary size, find a minimum core for H .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
statement_text: We say that Π L -reduces to Π' if there are two polynomial-time algorithms f , g , and constants α , β > 0 such that for each instance I of Π : Algorithm f produces an instance I' = f(I) of Π' , such that the optima of I and I' , OPT (I) and OPT (I') , respectively, satisfy OPT (I') ≤ α · OPT (I) Given any solution of I' with cost c' , algorithm g produces a solution of Π with cost c such that |c - OPT (I)| ≤ β |c' - OPT (I')| .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:set_cover
title: Set Cover
statement_text: Let U be a universe of n elements and let S = lbrace S_1,...,S_m rbrace be a subset of the power set of U satisfying cup_ i=1 ^m S_i = U . Then, given U and S , find a set cover T ⊆ S of minimum cardinality. Here, the defining property of a set cover is that cup_ S_i ∈ T S_i = U .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: Theorem:reduction_set-cover
statement_text: Set Cover L -reduces to MinCore.

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: corollary:hardness-MinCore
statement_text: MinCore cannot be approximated within a ratio (1-o(1)) · log n unless NP = P , where n = |V(H)| and m ∈ poly (n) .

title: MinCore _ radius
statement_text: Given a hypergraph H and a positive integer k . Is there a minimum core with radius ≤ k ?

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems

statement_text: MinCore _ radius is NP -hard for k ≥ 4 .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
statement_text: We define an m -leaf triangulation gadget as follows. Let T be a binary tree with m leaves where no vertex has one child. The m -leaf triangulation gadget Δ(T) is a 3-uniform hypergraph G = (V,E) whose vertices are those of T , and for every non-leaf vertex v of T , we add the edge lbrace v, c_1(v), c_2(v)rbrace , where c_1(v) is the left child and c_2(v) the right child from v .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: lemma:t-core
statement_text: Let Δ(T) be a triangulation gadget with root r and leaves v_1, ... v_m . Any C ⊆ {r,v_1, ... ,v_m} with | C | = 1 is a core of Δ(T) .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: lemma:triangulate-edge
statement_text: Let G=(V,E) a hypergraph with e ∈ E with | e | = m+1 . Let G'=(V' ⊇ V, E') be hypergraph in which e is replaced by Δ(T) , where T is a binary tree with external nodes e . G and G' have the same minimum core size.

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: theorem:3-uniform_hardness
statement_text: Set Cover L -reduces to 3-uniform MinCore.

statement_text: 3-uniform MinCore cannot be approximated within a ratio (1-o(1)) · log n , unless NP = P , where n = |V(H)| and m ∈ poly (n) .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
label: def:minrep
title: MINREP
statement_text: Let G=(A,B,E) be a bipartite graph with a partitioning of A and B into subsets A= cup_ i=1 ^ q_A , B= cup_ j=1 ^ q_A , where all A_i have size m_A and all B_i have size m_B . G induces a super-graph H=(A,B,E) with super-nodes A={A_1, ... ,A_ q_A } , B={B_1, ... ,B_ q_B } , and super-edges E ={A_iB_j | ∃ a ∈ A_i, b ∈ B_j: ab ∈ E} . We say a super-edge A_iB_j ∈ E is covered by ab ∈ E if a ∈ A_i and b ∈ B_j . The MINREP problem is to pick a minimum number of nodes A' ⊆ A,B' ⊆ B such that all super-edges are covered.

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
statement_text: MINREP cannot be approximated within ratio 2^ log ^ 1-ε n , for any ε>0 , unless NP=QP , where n= | V(G) | .

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
statement_text: We define the AND-gadget AND (U,v) = {V, E} as a hypergraph with V= U ∪ {x_1,x_2,v} and E={U + x_1, U+x_2, {x_1,x_2,v}} . We denote U as the set of input nodes, v as output node, and x_1,x_2 as inner nodes.

label: l:and

paper_title: Quantum k-SAT Related Hypergraph Problems
statement_text: MinCore cannot be approximated within ratio 2^ log ^ 1-ε n , for any ε>0 , unless NP=QP , where n= | E(G) | + | V(G) | .

statement_text: Let G = (V, E) be a hypergraph with minimum core size k for threshold function t and define G' = (V', E') with V' = V ∪ {s} and E' = {e ∪ {s} | e ∈ E}) . Then G' has minimum core size k+1 for threshold function t'(e) := t(e \ {s})+1 .
